**PSR proposes mandatory UK profit reporting for Visa and Mastercard**

*The Payment Systems Regulator is moving to require Visa and Mastercard to disclose detailed UK profitability data, a direct consequence of its finding that the card schemes face no effective competition.*

The PSR published a proposed direction and consultation on May 21 that would compel Visa and Mastercard to submit regular, detailed financial reports on their UK operations. The regulator wants granular data on revenues, costs and profits generated from card scheme and processing fees in the UK market, going beyond what the schemes currently disclose publicly.

This follows the PSR's final report on its market review of card scheme and processing fees, which concluded that Mastercard and Visa have increased fees without facing sufficient competitive constraint. The proposed reporting framework is designed to give the regulator an ongoing view of profitability, rather than relying on periodic market reviews to surface pricing concerns after the fact.

The consultation runs until later in the summer. If adopted, the direction would represent a significant increase in regulatory oversight of scheme economics in the UK, and could inform future interventions on pricing. For acquirers, merchants and competing payment methods, the resulting transparency may shift the terms of the debate around interchange and scheme fee levels.

*Sources: [UK regulator proposes profit reporting rules for Visa and Mastercard](https://www.reuters.com/world/uk/uk-regulator-proposes-profit-reporting-rules-visa-mastercard-2026-05-21/) — Reuters | [UK Regulator Proposes Profit Disclosure Rules for Visa, Mastercard](https://www.globalbankingandfinance.com/uk-regulator-proposes-profit-reporting-rules-visa-mastercard/) — Global Banking & Finance Review | [PSR publishes proposed direction and guidelines](https://www.regulationtomorrow.com/2026/05/psr-publishes-proposed-direction-and-guidelines-regulatory-financial-reporting-in-relation-to-the-market-review-of-card-scheme-and-processing-fees/) — Regulation Tomorrow*

**TrueLayer expands Dublin operations and appoints Ireland CEO**

*TrueLayer has named Pamela Fegan as its Ireland CEO and is expanding its Dublin office, signalling a deeper commitment to the Irish market as a European base for open banking payments.*

Fegan, who joins from a policy background in open banking, will lead TrueLayer's Irish operations. The company says it already powers more than 90 per cent of open banking payment volume through direct connectivity to all of Ireland's retail banks. The appointment and expansion come as TrueLayer positions Dublin as a hub for its European operations.

The move is notable in the context of post-Brexit regulatory geography. For UK-headquartered open banking firms, maintaining and growing an EU-licensed presence is operationally necessary. TrueLayer's choice to invest in Dublin, rather than simply maintain a licensing entity there, suggests the company sees Ireland as commercially significant in its own right, not just a passporting convenience.

Whether the Ireland CEO role is newly created or a replacement was not specified in the announcement. The hire does, however, coincide with a broader pattern of open banking providers building out dedicated country leadership as the sector matures beyond its UK origins.

*Sources: [TrueLayer Expands Dublin Operations and Appoints Pamela Fegan as Ireland CEO](https://financialit.net/news/people-moves/truelayer-expands-dublin-operations-and-appoints-pamela-fegan-ireland-ceo) — Financial IT*

**PSD3 and Payment Services Regulation near formal adoption**

*The European Parliament and Council have provisionally agreed the PSD3 and Payment Services Regulation texts, moving the legislative package into its final phase before publication.*

Glenbrook Partners flagged this week that the provisional political agreement between the European Parliament and EU Council brings PSD3 and the accompanying Payment Services Regulation materially closer to formal adoption. Once published in the Official Journal, member states will have a defined transposition period, typically 18 months for the directive component.

The shift from PSD2's single directive to a regulation-plus-directive structure is the most significant architectural change. The Payment Services Regulation will be directly applicable across the EU without national transposition, reducing the fragmentation that plagued PSD2 implementation. The directive element, PSD3, will handle authorisation and supervision of payment institutions.

For firms already planning their compliance programmes, the provisional agreement narrows the remaining uncertainty. The substantive policy content, covering such areas as open banking access, fraud liability, and strong customer authentication, is now largely settled. The remaining question is timing: how quickly the formal texts are published and when the transposition clock starts.

*Sources: [PSD3 Is Getting Closer for EU Banks](https://glenbrook.com/payments_news/psd3-is-getting-closer-for-eu-banks/) — Glenbrook Partners*

**Malaysia prepares phased open finance rollout with digital identity integration**

*Bank Negara Malaysia is planning to integrate national digital identity schemes with its open finance framework, offering a model for how emerging markets are building consent-driven data sharing from the outset.*

Bank Negara Malaysia disclosed that it sees scope for MyDigital ID and other personal data-sharing schemes to feed into the country's open finance ecosystem as it moves toward phased implementation. The central bank's approach ties identity verification directly into the data-sharing infrastructure, rather than treating them as separate regulatory workstreams.

This is a different trajectory from Europe and the UK, where open banking was built on top of existing identity and authentication frameworks and is now being extended toward broader open finance. Malaysia is attempting to build both layers simultaneously, which could reduce friction but also increases implementation complexity.

For European observers, the Malaysian approach is worth watching as a reference point. The EU's own open finance ambitions under the Financial Data Access framework face similar questions about how identity, consent and data portability interact. Markets that get the sequencing right early may avoid the retrofitting challenges that have characterised the European experience.

*Sources: [BNM sees potential for data sharing scheme integration with Open Finance framework](https://theedgemalaysia.com/node/804475) — The Edge Malaysia | [BNM Eyes MyDigital ID Link as Open Finance in Malaysia Takes Shape](https://fintechnews.my/58715/regtech-fintech-regulation-malaysia/open-finance-malaysia/) — Fintech News Malaysia*
